problems.nature: phishing and social engineering attacks via deceptive email content
problems.description: This problem involves detecting phishing and social engineering emails that use obfuscated text, suspicious URLs, and urgent language to trick users into clicking malicious links or divulging sensitive information. Attackers exploit trust by spoofing reputable brands or news sources and embedding URLs directing to fraudulent websites. Detection is challenged by variability in email sources, text-heavy content with both short and long bodies, and use of random or nonsensical word sequences to evade filters.
attack_vectors: email phishing via deceptive content and social engineering
malicious URLs directing to fraudulent websites
exploitation of user trust through impersonation of known brands or services

real_world_context.domain_insights: Phishing emails often feature unsolicited commercial offers related to health products or medications, suspicious URLs with uncommon or newly registered domains, and urgent or alarming language to provoke immediate action. Obfuscation techniques include gibberish text insertion and excessive whitespace irregularities. Attackers mimic payment suspension notices or fake newsletters to enhance credibility.
real_world_context.attack_sophistication: Moderate; attackers employ basic obfuscation such as random word sequences and urgency tactics but do not use advanced evasion like polymorphic content or zero-day exploits.
real_world_context.technical_implementation: Phishing emails embed URLs with suspicious domains often featuring uncommon TLDs or subdomains. The email body contains a high ratio of non-dictionary words (>20%), random text blocks, and repeated urgent call-to-action phrases. Subject lines are often very short or generic (e.g., 'Re:'). Spoofing techniques impersonate trusted brands or news sources to exploit user trust.
real_world_context.threat_landscape: Phishing remains a prevalent threat with campaigns promoting counterfeit goods, payment fraud, and social engineering themes such as sexual health and job offers. Multi-source campaigns indicate coordinated actor activity, complicating detection.
real_world_context.victim_impact: Users risk credential theft, financial loss, malware infection, and privacy breaches by interacting with malicious links or disclosing personal information.

attack_signatures: Emails promoting counterfeit or replica products with embedded URLs linking to suspicious domains
Phishing emails mimicking payment or account suspension notices urging users to update payment information
Use of random word sequences or gibberish text blocks within the email body
Social engineering content promising sexual performance enhancement or job offers requesting personal information
Fake newsletters or daily top 10 news digests with embedded malicious URLs and disclaimers
indicators_of_compromise: URLs with domains not matching known reputable sources, often with uncommon TLDs or subdomains
High ratio (>20%) of non-dictionary or gibberish words in body text
Subject lines shorter than 5 characters or generic terms like 'Re:'
Repeated urgent call-to-action phrases such as 'Click Here!', 'Guaranteed', or 'Payment failed'
Excessive line breaks and whitespace irregularities to obfuscate content
detection_criteria: Flag emails containing URLs with domains not in a trusted whitelist
Flag subject lines shorter than 5 characters or generic terms
Detect presence of urgent call-to-action phrases repeated more than once
Identify random or nonsensical word sequences embedded in body text
normal_vs_malicious: Benign emails contain coherent, relevant language with formal greetings and signatures
Benign URLs belong to well-known domains and are present in less than 10% of emails
Subject lines in benign emails are descriptive and longer than 5 characters
Benign emails lack urgent or alarmist language and have consistent formatting
Malicious emails show obfuscation, suspicious URLs, and urgency tactics
measurable_thresholds: Maximum allowed urgent call-to-action phrase occurrences: 1
URL domain whitelist enforcement: block unknown or suspicious domains
Maximum allowed random text block length: no more than 10 consecutive nonsensical words

attack_scenarios: An email claiming to be from a payment processor warns of account suspension and urges immediate update of payment details via an embedded suspicious URL with a newly registered domain.
A phishing email promoting counterfeit medications includes multiple obfuscated URLs and random gibberish text blocks to evade keyword filters.
A fake daily news digest spoofing a reputable news outlet like CNN contains embedded malicious links and disclaimers to appear legitimate, using short generic subject lines.
legitimate_scenarios: A community mailing list email with a detailed technical discussion, coherent paragraphs, formal greetings, and a descriptive subject line referencing a known project update.
A professional event announcement email containing structured content, contact information in the signature, and URLs linking only to well-known organizational domains.
A reply email within an established organization with consistent sender identifiers, no urgent language, and no suspicious URLs.

risk_reduction: Implement URL reputation filtering with strict whitelist and blacklist domain management
Use content-based spam filtering enhanced by NLP models to detect gibberish and obfuscation
Apply heuristic detection for urgency and repeated call-to-action phrases to flag suspicious emails
Employ multi-source correlation to identify coordinated phishing campaigns and spoofed senders
Regularly update detection rules and monitor domain registrations to identify emerging suspicious URLs
problems.detection_strategy: Combine URL domain reputation checks, gibberish text ratio analysis, subject line length validation, and detection of repeated urgent phrases using regex and NLP anomaly detection.
problems.monitoring_recommendation: Continuously track new domain registrations, frequency of urgent language in incoming emails, and source identifiers to proactively identify emerging phishing campaigns.

ratio of gibberish to dictionary words in body

frequency and phrasing of urgent call-to-action expressions
insertion of random or nonsensical word sequences
spoofed brand names and sender identifiers
pattern_preservation: embedding suspicious URLs with uncommon or newly registered domains
use of urgency and alarmist language repeated multiple times
random gibberish text blocks to simulate obfuscation

formal greetings and consistent formatting for benign samples
realism_requirements: maintain natural language coherence in benign emails
reflect multi-source variability in writing style and content length
simulate realistic sender spoofing and domain characteristics
include balanced class distribution with diverse attack scenarios
diversity_dimensions: source diversity reflecting multiple email origins
varied subject line complexity and style
different types of phishing themes (payment fraud, counterfeit goods, job offers)
varying degrees of text obfuscation and urgency levels
